topic_title: Why work? Needs of the individual
topic: 3.1 Why work? Needs of the individual

items.prompt: State two reasons why individuals work. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Two from: to earn income to meet living needs; security; social contact with other people; recognition; a sense of achievement; to develop their abilities.
marking_guidance: Point: People work for income to meet living needs, security, social contact, recognition, achievement and opportunities to develop their abilities.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between job security and social security. A worker expects her employment to continue; a separate benefit arrangement protects eligible workers against a specified income risk. [6]
items.canonical_answer: The expectation of continued employment is job security. The benefit arrangement is social security or protection. Confidence about keeping a job does not itself describe a benefit or insurance arrangement.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether higher pay alone addresses Nela’s stated motivation problem. Nela Repairs pays adequately and provides secure conditions, but experienced technicians complain that repetitive work gives them no responsibility or recognition. [8]
items.canonical_answer: Taylor emphasises financial incentives and systematic organisation of work. Maslow describes a hierarchy of physiological, safety, social, esteem and self-actualisation needs. Herzberg distinguishes hygiene or maintenance factors that prevent dissatisfaction from motivators within the work itself. These theories suggest different reasons for behaviour and different responses. Pay and safe conditions matter, but they may not provide achievement, recognition or responsibility. Use the theory that explains the stated problem, identify its limits and assess the workforce rather than mixing categories from different theorists. Needs need not follow a rigid identical order for every person. A manager should investigate and review the response instead of treating a theory as proof that one measure will motivate everyone. Herzberg suggests addressing the work itself through meaningful responsibility and recognition. More pay could be welcomed but does not directly resolve the stated complaint. Choose job improvement with staff consultation; basic pay still matters if later evidence shows it is inadequate.
marking_guidance: Knowledge: Taylor emphasises financial incentives and systematic organisation of work.

items.prompt: Explain the distinction in Herzberg’s theory: Ula Print repairs unsafe conditions and separately gives experienced staff responsibility for checking completed work. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Safer working conditions address a hygiene or maintenance factor and can reduce dissatisfaction. Meaningful responsibility addresses a motivator. Hygiene and maintenance name the same category here, not two separate theories. Neither classification is Maslow’s hierarchy or Taylor’s output-pay model.

items.prompt: State two features of Taylor’s approach to work. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Systematic analysis of tasks to find an efficient method; financial incentives linked to measurable output.
marking_guidance: Point: Systematic analysis of tasks to find an efficient method; financial incentives linked to measurable output.

items.prompt: Explain how Taylor’s approach could affect Tula’s packers. Tula Packs can count correctly completed packs and workers control the pace within safe limits. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Taylor’s scientific-management approach examines tasks systematically, seeks an efficient method, selects suitable workers and links financial reward to output. Piece-rate pay can reward additional acceptable units, making a clear effort–earnings link where output is measurable and workers can influence it. The approach gives money a central role rather than explaining motivation through a hierarchy of needs. Its limits include neglecting social needs and job satisfaction, and encouraging speed at the expense of quality or safety if targets are poorly designed. It suits some repetitive measurable work better than complex team services where individual output is difficult to attribute. An output-linked reward may encourage more acceptable packs, but quality checks and attainable targets are needed. Paying for rejected packs would reward the wrong result.
marking_guidance: Knowledge: Taylor’s scientific-management approach examines tasks systematically, seeks an efficient method, selects suitable workers and links financial reward to output.

items.prompt: Explain how Maslow helps explain the different needs of Hema’s workers. Hema Services’ new worker is worried about unreliable earnings, while an experienced colleague wants opportunities to develop skills. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Maslow’s hierarchy identifies physiological needs such as basic living requirements, safety needs such as secure and safe work, social needs such as belonging, esteem needs such as recognition and self-actualisation through developing potential. Pay can help basic needs, secure conditions support safety, team relationships support social needs, praise can support esteem and challenging opportunities can support development. The model suggests unmet needs influence motivation, with lower needs commonly receiving attention before higher ones. Do not assume every worker follows an identical fixed sequence or stops valuing money after one need is met. Managers need to identify which needs matter in the particular case. Reliable pay can help the first worker’s basic needs, while suitable developmental work can address the colleague’s higher-level aspirations. One uniform reward may not fit both.
marking_guidance: Knowledge: Maslow’s hierarchy identifies physiological needs such as basic living requirements, safety needs such as secure and safe work, social needs such as belonging, esteem needs such as recognition and self-actualisation through developing potential.

items.prompt: Explain how Herzberg distinguishes Oha’s work-content problem from a hygiene issue. Oha Design staff have safe conditions and fair supervision, but are not allowed to make creative choices on their own projects and receive no recognition when projects are completed. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Herzberg distinguishes hygiene or maintenance factors, including pay, conditions, supervision and policies, from motivators such as achievement, recognition, responsibility, advancement and the work itself. Poor hygiene factors can create dissatisfaction; putting them right can remove that dissatisfaction without necessarily producing lasting motivation. Motivators concern positive satisfaction from meaningful work. Job enrichment can add genuine responsibility and challenge rather than merely more repetitive tasks. The model does not justify ignoring wages or claiming that every employee responds identically. Diagnose the actual complaint and avoid labelling Maslow’s hierarchy or Taylor’s output incentives as Herzberg’s categories. Giving capable staff responsibility for design choices and recognising achievement targets motivators. Fixing a broken chair would address a hygiene problem, which is worthwhile but different.
marking_guidance: Knowledge: Herzberg distinguishes hygiene or maintenance factors, including pay, conditions, supervision and policies, from motivators such as achievement, recognition, responsibility, advancement and the work itself.

items.prompt:
Ena Repairs pays adequately and provides safe, secure work. Skilled staff report repetitive tasks and no recognition. The manager compares a further general pay rise with meaningful responsibility and recognition.

a(i) State two reasons people work. [2]
a(ii) State one hygiene factor and one motivator from Herzberg. [2]
b State two non-financial needs work can satisfy. [2]
c Explain why Herzberg suggests a work-content response at Ena. [6]
d Evaluate a further general pay rise against meaningful responsibility and recognition. [8]
items.canonical_answer: a(i) Income and job security. a(ii) Working conditions are hygiene; achievement is a motivator. b Social contact and personal development. c Adequate pay and safe conditions address hygiene factors, while the stated repetitive work and lack of recognition concern motivators. Genuine responsibility can provide achievement and a more satisfying role; recognition acknowledges that achievement. d Further pay may be welcome but does not directly change repetitive work. Responsibility and recognition address the stated unmet need, though staff need capability and support. Choose that response and review satisfaction. Reconsider pay if evidence shows it is inadequate; do not infer that money has no value.

items.prompt:
Ena Repairs pays adequately and provides safe, secure work. Skilled staff report repetitive tasks and no recognition. The manager compares a further general pay rise with meaningful responsibility and recognition.

a Explain how Maslow and Herzberg could account for Ena’s staff concerns without mixing their categories. [8]
b Evaluate whether Taylor’s financial-incentive emphasis is the best response here. [12]
items.canonical_answer: a Maslow can interpret the concerns as esteem and development needs beyond the stated basic pay and safety provision. Herzberg instead distinguishes adequate hygiene from missing motivators such as recognition and meaningful work. Both can support investigating work content, but a need level is not a Herzberg factor label. b Output-linked pay can encourage measurable additional effort where workers control output and quality is protected. Here the complaint is repetitive work and recognition, not an inadequate effort–earnings link. A financial incentive could leave the complaint unresolved and put pressure on speed. Prefer meaningful responsibility with support and recognition, monitor the outcome and retain fair pay. A measurable production problem with clear financial dissatisfaction would strengthen Taylor’s relevance; those conditions are not stated.

items.prompt:
Tara Print pays reliably at a level staff describe as adequate. Experienced staff want more say in completing their work. Management compares another pay rise with meaningful responsibility.

Evaluate another pay rise against meaningful responsibility at Tara. Give a concise plan. [12]
items.canonical_answer: Needs: income matters, but staff describe pay as adequate and ask for more say. Herzberg: pay is hygiene; genuine responsibility is a motivator. Maslow: responsibility may support esteem and development. Alternative: a pay rise may be valued but leaves control over the work unchanged. Judgement: offer supported responsibility and review outcomes; do not assume all staff seek identical changes or that pay can be ignored.

items.prompt:
Tara Print pays reliably at a level staff describe as adequate. Experienced staff want more say in completing their work. Management compares another pay rise with meaningful responsibility. For part (b) only, staff now face delayed wages that prevent them meeting basic living costs. Other facts remain unchanged.

a Evaluate the two approaches at Tara under the original facts. [12]
b Evaluate priorities after wages are delayed. Explain whether the original judgement changes. [12]
items.canonical_answer: a Reliable adequate pay and a request for more say favour genuine responsibility, consistent with Herzberg’s motivators and Maslow’s esteem/development needs. Support staff competence and keep fair conditions; more pay alone leaves the stated work-control concern. b Delayed wages create an immediate basic-income problem. Restore reliable pay first: Maslow highlights basic needs and Herzberg identifies a hygiene failure causing dissatisfaction. Responsibility remains worthwhile but cannot buy food or replace wages due. The priority changes because the original adequate-pay condition has failed; once corrected, address work content as well.
